title: II. The Alarm
paragraphs: Our police captain, Mihail Makarovitch Makarov, was a retired lieutenant-colonel and a widower, and a thoroughly good man. He had lived among us only three years, yet everyone thought well of him, chiefly because he “knew how to keep society together.” He always had visitors and couldn’t have lived without them. Someone was forever dining at his house, and he never sat down to a meal alone. He also gave regular dinners, on all sorts of occasions, some of them quite surprising. The food wasn’t _recherché_, but there was plenty of it. The fish pies were excellent, and the wine made up in quantity for what it lacked in quality.

Guests came first into a well-furnished billiard room. On its walls hung pictures of English racehorses in black frames, a decoration every bachelor’s billiard room must have, as we all know. Cards were played there every evening, if only at a single table. Often, though, the whole society of our town gathered at his house to dance, mammas and young ladies and all. Mihail Makarovitch was a widower, but he didn’t live alone. His widowed daughter lived with him, along with her two unmarried daughters. They were grown girls who had finished their schooling, pleasant-looking and lively. Everyone knew they would have no dowry, yet they still drew all the fashionable young men to their grandfather’s house.

Mihail Makarovitch was not very efficient at his work, though he did it no worse than many others. To put it plainly, he was a man of rather limited education. He could not always be trusted to know where his official powers ended. He didn’t exactly fail to understand certain reforms of the present reign. Rather, he made glaring blunders when he interpreted them. This wasn’t because he was especially dull. He was careless, and always too hurried to look into the matter properly.

“I have the heart of a soldier, not a civilian,” he used to say of himself. He had never formed a clear idea of the basic principles behind the reforms connected with the emancipation of the serfs. He simply picked them up from year to year, so to speak, and added to what he knew through practice, without ever meaning to. And he was a landowner himself, too. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain that he would find some of Mihail Makarovitch’s visitors there that evening, but he didn’t know which ones. As it happened, the prosecutor was at that moment playing whist at the captain’s with Varvinsky, our district doctor. Varvinsky was a young man who had just come to us from Petersburg, where he had taken a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, was really only the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor. He was a rather peculiar man, about thirty-five, inclined to consumption, and married to a fat, childless wife. He was vain and irritable, though he had a good mind and even a kind heart. The trouble with him seemed to be only this: he thought himself abler than he was. That made him seem constantly ill at ease. He also had higher, even artistic, leanings, toward psychology for instance, toward a special study of the human heart and a special knowledge of the criminal and his crime. He felt wronged on this account. He believed he had been passed over in the service, and he was firmly convinced that in higher circles he was not properly valued and had enemies. In gloomy moments he even threatened to resign and take up criminal cases as a barrister. The unexpected Karamazov case stirred him deeply: “It was a case that might well be talked about all over Russia.” But I am running ahead.

The young investigating lawyer, Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, had come from Petersburg only two months before. He was sitting in the next room with the young ladies. Afterwards people talked about it and wondered that all these gentlemen should have gathered, as if by design, at the house of the chief authority on the very evening of “the crime.” Yet the explanation was perfectly simple, and it all came about quite naturally.

Ippolit Kirillovitch’s wife had had toothache for two days, and he had gone out to get away from her groans. The doctor, being what he was, could not spend an evening anywhere but at cards. As for Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, he had been meaning for three days to drop in at Mihail Makarovitch’s that evening, as if by chance. His plan was to give the eldest granddaughter, Olga Mihailovna, a sly surprise. He would show her that he knew her secret: that it was her birthday, and that she was purposely hiding it so she wouldn’t have to give a dance. He looked forward to a great deal of fun, with many playful jokes about her age and her fear of telling it, about how he knew her secret and would tell everybody, and so on. The charming young man was a past master at such teasing. The ladies had named him “the naughty man,” and he seemed delighted with the name. Still, he was extremely well-bred, of good family, education and feelings. Though he lived for pleasure, his jests were always innocent and in good taste. He was short and delicate-looking, and on his white, slender, small fingers he always wore several big, glittering rings. When he was busy with his official duties, he turned extraordinarily solemn, as if he understood his position and the sacredness of the obligations laid on him. He had a special gift for baffling murderers and other criminals of the peasant class when he questioned them. If he didn’t win their respect, he certainly managed to make them wonder.

Pyotr Ilyitch was simply dumbfounded when he walked into the police captain’s house. He saw at once that everyone knew. They had actually thrown down their cards and were all on their feet, talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had left the young ladies and come running in, looking keyed up and ready for action. The news that met Pyotr Ilyitch was astounding: old Fyodor Pavlovitch really had been murdered that evening in his own house, murdered and robbed. The news had reached them only a moment before, and this is how it came.

Marfa Ignatyevna was the wife of old Grigory, the man who had been knocked senseless by the fence. She was sleeping soundly in her bed, and after the dose of medicine she had taken she might well have slept till morning. But suddenly she woke up. A fearful epileptic scream from Smerdyakov, who lay unconscious in the next room, had no doubt roused her. That scream always came before his fits, and it always frightened and upset Marfa Ignatyevna. She had never been able to get used to it. She jumped up and ran, half asleep, to Smerdyakov’s room. It was dark there, and she could only hear the sick man beginning to gasp and thrash about. Then Marfa Ignatyevna herself cried out and was about to call her husband. But she suddenly realized that he had not been in bed beside her when she got up. She ran back to the bed and groped about with her hands, and the bed was indeed empty. So he must have gone out—but where? She ran to the steps and called him timidly. Of course there was no answer, but far off in the garden, in the darkness, she heard groans. She listened. The groans came again, and it was plain they were coming from the garden.
“Good Lord! It’s just like what happened with Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!” she thought in confusion. She went timidly down the steps and saw that the garden gate stood open.
“He must be out there, poor dear,” she thought. She went up to the gate, and all at once she heard Grigory clearly, calling her by name: “Marfa! Marfa!” His voice was weak, moaning and dreadful.

“Lord, protect us!” Marfa Ignatyevna murmured. She ran toward the voice, and that was how she found Grigory. But he was not by the fence where he had been struck down. He was about twenty paces away. It came out later that when he came to himself he had crawled off, and he had probably taken a long time to get so far, losing consciousness several times. She saw at once that he was covered in blood, and she screamed at the top of her voice. Grigory was muttering, barely making sense:
“He’s murdered ... his father murdered.... Why scream, silly ... run ... get somebody....”

But Marfa kept on screaming. She saw that her master’s window was open and a candle was alight in it, so she ran over and began calling Fyodor Pavlovitch. But when she looked in at the window, she saw a fearful sight. Her master lay on his back on the floor, not moving. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked in blood. The candle on the table brightly lit up the blood and the still, dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch. Terror-stricken, Marfa rushed from the window and out of the garden. She drew the bolt of the big gate and ran headlong, by the back way, to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Mother and daughter were both asleep, but Marfa’s desperate, unceasing screams and her knocking at the shutter woke them. Shrieking and screaming incoherently, Marfa still managed to tell them the main fact and beg for help. As it happened, Foma had come back from his wanderings and was spending the night with them. They got him up at once, and all three ran to the scene of the crime. On the way Marya Kondratyevna remembered that about eight o’clock she had heard a dreadful scream from the garden next door. That must have been Grigory’s scream of “Parricide!” uttered when he caught hold of Mitya’s leg.

“One person screamed out and then it went quiet,” Marya Kondratyevna explained as she ran. They ran to the spot where Grigory lay, and the two women, with Foma’s help, carried him to the lodge. They lit a candle and saw that Smerdyakov was no better. He was writhing in convulsions, his eyes fixed in a squint, with foam running from his lips. They wet Grigory’s forehead with water and vinegar, and the water brought him round at once. Right away he asked:
“Is the master murdered?”

Then Foma and both women ran to the house. This time they saw that not only the window but also the door into the garden was wide open. Yet for the last week Fyodor Pavlovitch had locked himself in every night and had not let even Grigory in, whatever the excuse. Seeing that door open, they were afraid to go in to Fyodor Pavlovitch, “for fear something might happen afterwards.” When they went back to Grigory, the old man told them to go straight to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna ran there and gave the alarm to the whole company at the captain’s. She arrived only five minutes before Pyotr Ilyitch. So his story did not come as his own guess and theory. It came as direct confirmation, from a witness, of the theory everyone held about who the criminal was. (Deep in his heart he had refused to believe that theory until that moment.)

They resolved to act with energy. The deputy police inspector of the town was commissioned to take four witnesses, go into Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, and open an inquiry on the spot, following the regular forms, which I will not go into here. The district doctor, a zealous man new to his work, almost insisted on going with the police captain, the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer.

I will say briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found quite dead, his skull smashed in. But with what? Most probably with the same weapon that had struck Grigory. And the moment that weapon was found, Grigory, who was at once given all possible medical help, told in a weak, breaking voice how he had been knocked down. They searched with a lantern by the fence and found the brass pestle, dropped in a most conspicuous place on the garden path. In the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch lay, there was no sign of disorder. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up from the floor a big, thick envelope. On it was written: “A present of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she is willing to come.” Below that Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, “For my little chicken.” The envelope bore three seals of red sealing wax, but it had been torn open and was empty: the money had been taken. On the floor they also found a piece of narrow pink ribbon, which had been tied around the envelope.

One part of Pyotr Ilyitch’s evidence made a great impression on the prosecutor and the investigating magistrate. This was his idea that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would shoot himself before daybreak. Dmitri had resolved to do it, he had told Ilyitch so, he had taken the pistols and loaded them in front of him, he had written a letter and put it in his pocket, and so on. Pyotr Ilyitch still couldn’t quite believe it, and he had threatened to tell someone to prevent the suicide. Mitya had answered, grinning: “You’ll be too late.” So they must hurry to Mokroe and find the criminal before he really did shoot himself.
“That’s clear, that’s clear!” the prosecutor said again and again, in great excitement. “That’s exactly how these madmen go on: ‘I’ll kill myself tomorrow, so I’ll make merry until I die!’”
The story of how Mitya had bought the wine and provisions excited the prosecutor more than ever.

“Remember the fellow who murdered the merchant Olsufyev, gentlemen? He stole fifteen hundred, went straight off to have his hair curled, and then, without even hiding the money, carrying it almost in his hand like that, he went off to the girls.”

But the inquiry, the search and the formalities in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house held them all up. It took time, and so they sent someone ahead to Mokroe two hours before they set out. This was the officer of the rural police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who had come into town the morning before to collect his pay. His orders were not to raise the alarm when he reached Mokroe. He was to keep constant watch over the “criminal” until the proper authorities arrived, and to find witnesses for the arrest, police constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did as he was told. He kept his identity secret and gave no one the slightest hint of his secret business, except his old acquaintance Trifon Borissovitch. He had spoken to him just before Mitya met the landlord on the balcony, looking for him in the dark, and he noticed at once a change in Trifon Borissovitch’s face and voice. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew he was being watched. Trifon Borissovitch had carried off the box with the pistols and put it in a suitable place. Only after four o’clock, almost at sunrise, did all the officials arrive, the police captain, the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer, in two carriages each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, to carry out a post-mortem on the body next day. But he was especially interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.

“Epileptic fits as violent and long as these, coming one after another for twenty-four hours, are seldom seen, and they are of interest to science,” he declared enthusiastically to his companions. As they left, they laughingly congratulated him on his find. The prosecutor and the investigating lawyer clearly remembered the doctor saying that Smerdyakov could not live through the night.
After these long but, I think, necessary explanations, we will go back to the point in our tale where we broke off.
